title: Normalize caller-owned options without writing results back into them
applies_when: A public connection or table-creation API normalizes caller-owned options, storage maps or typed overrides, including frozen inputs and options reused across calls; or an HTTP transport injects headers into a caller-owned request.
lesson: A functional normalization helper does not make its caller non-mutating: assigning its returned map to an aliased options object still changes caller state. Trace both the outer object and nested map. Build a local normalized options object, and merge overrides into a local map when that merge would mutate the input. Test frozen outer options with and without a nested map, frozen nested maps, and repeated real API calls that preserve input contents and identity. Retain an already-copying overload as a passing control so the regression isolates the ownership violation. Exercise the native operation after normalization rather than testing a copied expression alone. For Go RoundTripper header injection, WithContext is only a shallow request copy: sequential calls can retain a previous conversation header through the shared map. Clone the request before setting headers, preserve outbound injection, and test an explicitly empty context override after closing each response. Also mutate an outbound header value slice to check that the original values no longer alias it.
avoid_when: An explicitly documented in-place builder may own and modify its input. A shallow object spread does not isolate later writes to nested objects; copy the specific nested map where needed, not every object or opaque handle. Go Request.Clone does not deep-copy Body, and RoundTripper is allowed to consume and close it; do not generalize header isolation into body ownership changes or test concurrent request reuse as if supported. Preserving caller input does not prove option precedence, native lifetime, concurrency, all overloads or performance. Released native libraries do not establish current-head native-build compatibility, and an open PR or fork branch is not a merged fix.

evidence.note: Exact proposed connection fix copies the outer options before assigning the normalized storage map; URI and namespace entry points previously aliased caller options, while the object overload already copied them.

Public native-database regressions cover frozen and reused inputs. Contributor reproduction reports six affected entry-point failures and three unchanged overload controls before the entry fix, then 52 passing tests afterward.

Open correctness PR also keeps table-creation storage merges local and preserves typed option precedence. Validation uses current TypeScript with a released native library plus strict matching-release checks; no current-head Rust/native rebuild, GPU or performance claim.

Pinned upstream transport injects provider and conversation headers directly into the caller's request. This implementation path lets the existing source-affinity reader find the scoped ownership lesson; the source link alone is not a runtime or production-prevalence result.

The documented transport contract preserves request fields except consuming/closing Body; callers wait until the response Body is closed before reuse. Request.WithContext is shallow while Request.Clone deep-copies headers but not Body. Mechanism, not a security or performance claim.

Contributor-native Linux amd64 Go1.27.2 validation of actual goraven/util and real pinned modules: original b176662 source plus identical focused tests gives 2 regression failures and 3 passes; the one-line Request.Clone repair gives 5 passes. Full util ordinary/race each gives 59 passing test/subtest events, no failures/skips, and vet/gofmt pass. Source and go.mod/go.sum postchecks match frozen bytes. Not whole application, debug-mode coverage, Windows/minimum-Go/CI, security impact, performance, maintainer acceptance or prospective selector benefit.
